Name: reasoning_language_typology
Title: Does the Language of Thought Matter? Probing How Linguistic Typology Shapes LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: The specific natural language in which an LLM externalizes its chain-of-thought is not a neutral carrier but causally shapes its reasoning accuracy, and typological features of that language (morphological richness, word order, numeral systems, tense/aspect marking) systematically predict reasoning performance on structurally-matched tasks—revealing that 'intelligence' in LLMs is partly a linguistic artifact rather than a language-independent capacity.
Related Work: Prior work on CoT (Wei et al.), CoT necessity/faithfulness (Chain-of-Probe, Causal Sufficiency & Necessity, Brown-Cohen et al. on opaque serial depth) treats reasoning traces as English-language artifacts and studies WHEN CoT is needed, not WHICH language it should be in. Multilingual reasoning work (e.g., cross-lingual CoT, MGSM) shows English-CoT often outperforms native-language CoT but attributes this only to training-data imbalance. No work isolates the causal effect of a language's structural/typological properties on reasoning while controlling for content difficulty, nor tests whether typological features predict where reasoning succeeds or fails. Our proposal reframes the language↔intelligence question typologically and causally, distinguishing it from data-quantity explanations.
Abstract: Large language models externalize reasoning as text, almost always studied in English. But does the language of thought itself change what a model can reason about? We investigate whether typological properties of the language used for chain-of-thought reasoning—morphological richness, dominant word order, numeral/base systems, and tense-aspect marking—causally affect reasoning accuracy, independent of how much training data existed for that language. We construct controlled 'typology-matched' reasoning suites: parallel problem sets (arithmetic, temporal ordering, spatial/relational, syllogistic) rendered into 12 languages spanning contrasting typological features, holding semantic content and difficulty fixed via back-translation verification. We prompt open multilingual LLMs (Qwen, Aya, Llama-3, Gemma) to reason in each target language and measure accuracy, controlling for training-data frequency using published corpus statistics as a covariate in mixed-effects regression. Crucially, we run intervention experiments: forcing reasoning in a language whose numeral base (e.g., French vigesimal '80=quatre-vingts', or vigesimal counting languages) mismatches the arithmetic task, and comparing to matched languages, to isolate structural effects from data effects. We further test whether translating only the reasoning trace (not the question) between typologically distinct languages changes correctness. We hypothesize that structural features predict systematic error patterns (e.g., languages with transparent numeral systems yield fewer arithmetic errors; SOV languages differ on relational reasoning), demonstrating that LLM 'intelligence' is partially a linguistic artifact. Findings would inform reasoning-language selection, cross-lingual fairness, and theories of language-thought coupling in AI.
Experiments: 1) BUILD typology-matched benchmark: take ~300 base problems across 4 categories (multi-digit arithmetic, temporal event ordering, spatial/kinship relational reasoning, categorical syllogisms). Render each into 12 languages selected to systematically vary typological axes (numeral base: decimal vs vigesimal-influenced e.g. French/Danish; word order: SVO/SOV/VSO; morphological richness: analytic Mandarin vs agglutinative Turkish vs fusional Russian; tense-aspect explicitness). Verify semantic equivalence via round-trip translation + human/automated checks on a sample. 2) MAIN EFFECT: for each of 4 open multilingual LLMs, prompt to solve+reason in each target language; measure final-answer accuracy and category-specific error taxonomy. 3) CONTROL for data frequency: obtain per-language token counts (e.g., from public corpus stats / CC statistics) and fit mixed-effects logistic regression: accuracy ~ typology_features + log(data_freq) + (1|problem) + (1|model), testing whether typology features remain significant after controlling for data. 4) INTERVENTION A (numeral mismatch): compare arithmetic accuracy when reasoning in transparent-numeral vs opaque-numeral languages matched on data frequency; predict transparent-numeral advantage. 5) INTERVENTION B (trace-only translation): keep question in English, force the CoT in language L, measure accuracy vs English-CoT; and translate a correct English CoT into L and back, checking answer stability. 6) CROSS-CATEGORY: test whether word-order/morphology features interact with relational vs arithmetic tasks (predicted double dissociation). METRICS: accuracy, error-type distribution, regression coefficient significance/effect sizes for typology features, and consistency (agreement rate across languages on same problem). Compute a 'linguistic sensitivity index' per model = variance in accuracy across languages after data-frequency correction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Confounding: training-data quantity and quality per language is hard to fully control; we mitigate with regression covariates but residual confounds remain. 2) Translation artifacts could introduce difficulty differences; mitigated by round-trip verification and matched-content design. 3) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes. 4) Tokenizer differences across languages could partly drive results—we treat this as part of the 'linguistic' effect but analyze it separately. 5) Typological features are correlated across languages, limiting clean isolation of any single feature; addressed via careful language selection maximizing orthogonal variation. 6) Causal claims from observational cross-language comparisons are limited, hence the explicit intervention experiments.
